title: Inside the Memory Supercycle's Second Act
body_markdown:
Memory contract prices are rising at roughly a fifth of the rate they were two quarters ago. That is the most misleading number in the market right now.


‍


Conventional DRAM contract prices rose 90–95% quarter over quarter in Q1 2026, a record. Q2 came in at 58–63%. Server DRAM is forecast at 13–18% for Q3. Spot prices have not slowed at all: the mainstream DDR4 8Gb chip reached $42.08 on July 28, up from $33.02 in early March, with no sustained multi-week decline since April.


‍


The shortage has not eased. It has split, and which side of it you are on is now decided by paperwork rather than by what you buy.


## Three things changed since April


**Long-term agreements are rerouting the increases.** The major cloud providers have locked in contracts, so their pricing is contractually capped. TrendForce expects the remaining pressure to shift toward buyers without those agreements, and contract prices are still forecast to rise every quarter through the second half of 2027.


‍


**DDR4 and DDR5 are converging.** DDR4 still trades at a 65–67% premium per gigabyte over DDR5, but that premium was about 82% in April. DDR5 16Gb rose 36.1% since our last edition against 23.8% for DDR4, so the sharper tightening this quarter happened one generation up.


‍


**2027 is a supply problem.** SK hynix expects it to be the worst supply year in the industry's history, and the KRW 54.3 trillion it approved on August 7 delivers its first cleanroom in June 2029. None of the capacity being funded now adds a bit to 2026.
